— Conflicting opinions and research outcomes

d1 and d5 present evidence that most birds do not mate for life and that monogamy often includes extra-pair behavior, while d2, d4, d6, and d8 highlight species commonly described as mating for life. d10 clarifies that “monogamous” often refers to seasonal rather than lifelong bonds, and d11 shows even socially lifelong species may cheat. This set contains mutually exclusive claims about prevalence and faithfulness, fitting the “Conflicting opinions and research outcomes” label.

The evidence collectively shows two incompatible narratives: one that most birds are not lifelong, faithful mates and another that many species form lifelong bonds. These perspectives cannot be reconciled without dismissing one side’s core claims, which is consistent with the given conflict type.

Birds’ mating systems vary widely: some species form lifelong pair bonds, while most do not mate for life and often engage in extra-pair mating within socially monogamous relationships [d1,d5]. A contrasting view emphasizes that many iconic species (e.g., swans, albatrosses, penguins, bald eagles) are described as mating for life [d2,d4,d6,d8]. Even within lifelong pairings, behaviors such as “cheating” or extra-pair copulation have been documented, further complicating the picture [d1,d11]. Terminology also differs, with “monogamous” sometimes referring only to seasonal bonds rather than lifelong fidelity [d10].
